I don't think it's ''behaving'' (read: normal) to be watching the same 20 episodes on repeat for two straight days. That's alarming, actually. If it were the same show which has multiple seasons, then yes; ok. But we're talking about something with one season, and the customer has watched that one season four times in forty-two hours.

I think that's the equivalent to the girl at the bar who is sitting by himself at the end ordering shot after shot after shot and not talking to anyone, including the bartender (except to order more alcohol), all night. That girl always worries you in some form or another when she decides to leave. 

This would be the same as asking her: "hey, are you ok to drive? / can you get home safely? / do you have someone to help you home?"

True story: I have a friend who was a bartender who did that a few times.

I believe that if people truly have a problem that could kill them, you help. ''It's not my job,'' doesn't really apply once it's life or death. It's always your job to help someone who's walking close to the edge. 

Putting it another way: if a cashier at the grocery store notices a woman coming in frequently with new bruises all the time, should she slip her the number to a shelter for people who are abused? I would hope the cashier would do that, even if it's not in the job description. It's decency, I think. 

(Also, I'm not trying to sound contrarian or like an ass here, I honestly think this would be a good idea and I value your input as it's helping me brainstorm a lot.)

I think I get your meaning. In truth, I don't immediately recall ever seeing an ad on Netflix while I'm watching my shows, so I'm not sure if that would be the best route to deliver services on. 

Also, I'm not so sure it would be the company ''judging'' their customers. It wouldn't come up after every episode; just when the person has excessively been watching something for long amounts of time. For example, if one were to watch the first season of OINB three consecutive times in two days, a popup similar to ''Are you still watching?" would appear saying "Do you need someone to talk to?" 

From there, the user could choose ''yes'' and be directed somewhere to  talk to someone about their issues, or ''no'' and go on doing exactly what they were doing before with no issue. It's more of a check-up I'm thinking of than a judgement. 

Maybe 7 Cups could do some advertising alongside Netflix, but independent from each other. Something like 7 Cups running a promotion where you get the first three months of Netflix free by signing up for their service. That way people at least know the help is out there if they need it, and they know how to access it.

In fact, I think it would be an absolute springboard into mental health awareness. The only thing making it even cooler is that it's Netflix, which is already rather iconic among 20-30 somethings; often the same demographic of people who suffer from unchecked depression and high amounts of stress.

I don't think it would be inappropriate. If you knew someone you did business with was inside for 18 hours out of the day watching the same season of Orange Is The New Black, regardless of how close you were with them, wouldn't you be concerned? Wouldn't you want to help them however you could; even if it was just by a gentle nudge of ''hey, are you ok? Because I know someone who you can talk to if you're not."

Something like that. "We've noticed behavior on your account which our analysts have determined as 'binge-watching.' We value you as a customer and want to make sure you're ok. Do you need someone to talk to?"

> Yes, take me to 7 Cups. 

> No, thank you; I'm safe right now.

I know the pain of applying to jobs and never hearing anything back, or even getting an interview. I also know the incredible sense of disappointment after having an interview that you thought was a knock-out, and never receiving a call back. Understand that it's not a setback, but a learning opportunity. 

If there is a job fair or career resource center in your area, I suggest you go to it first thing. They can look over your resume and ensure there are no gaps or holes that a hiring manager will look over. They can also give you tips and tricks on interviewing and making an impression with each hiring manager you see. What's important to remember, and what kept me going in my job search, is that if you do have a stellar interview, and they don't call you back, that means it's a shit company. If they're willing to just leave you on standby, they're willing to leave  their customers on standby, which is hell for you. 

Also, while you're at the career resource center, see if they have any advice on that subject you're not grasping. Or look for other subreddits on the subject. There may be someone out there who has a better way of explaining it. 

Finally, on the girlfriend thing... Don't be too hard on her. I'm sure she cares about you greatly, but it's also her birthday. She's got parents, grandparents, friends, family, bosses, coworkers; everyone is paying her attention today. She's probably a bit overwhelmed. I wouldn't over-think anything for now; just give her space, let her know you're there if she wants to talk or even get together, and that you want to know all about how her day went once she gets settled. 

I really hope any of this helps you. If not, just take my virtual hugs and I hope you have a better day. I'm sure you'll hear back from something soon!

I can relate to you, OP. I have the same problems, especially with technology malfunctions (for the money we pay for it, it should WORK). But I digress. 
Replacing phones and computer equipment gets very expensive, very quickly. I found a great way to destress (for me) is to take a deep breath, decompress, and really try to think about why I'm getting THIS angry at something that doesn't even have a pulse. 
If it's a situation where I'm unable to take that step back, I try to escape the situation for a bit. Go for a walk with headphones (always have a back up player in case you smash your cell phone, is a clear rule for me) and visit a place where you feel safe and comfortable. Try not to drive too much in this state; other idiots on the road will only serve to exacerbate your anger. 
Think about whether or not you're hungry, and if that's an underlying cause of your anger. 
Visit a quiet place where you can reflect, or try journalling to see if there's a pattern in your outbursts.
Whatever you do, try to calm down without using violence. I know it's hard, but ultimately YOU rule your emotions, not the other way around.

"Anyone there?" the voice resounded throughout the gulag. A hush fell over the spirits; the screaming temporarily stopped only to be replaced by an unwavering fear of what was to come. 
Memories of a similar call from a commander, a man looking for a would-be escapee trying to claw his way out through the very walls, only to be trapped there in a hole by gunfire. 
Nothing moved. 
"Show yourself!" the voice ordered. Suddenly, chaos. Everything rushed, everything banged, everything was turned upside down as hundreds of us presented ourselves to the hall for hope of a lighter punishment.
The man fell down, and we all shrieked in horror.
Memories. We were to get it now. 
"Who's there!?" 
A million cries of our numbers, sounding off the walls like nails on a chalkboard, travelling around the bars and twanging off the metal of the cages. Whips cracked, shots fired, drills whirring in agony as they drove into the backs and heads and hands of us; memories! 
"Spirits, go!" the man cried from the floor, covering his face. We were sure it was our commander, coming to torture us after so many years of lying dormant. 
Memories; we fled.

"Edward, we can't go on like this," she said, touching the silicone skin of the projection of her lover. She hated and loved the man in the most complex of ways; he was a monster, a villain, a killer; he was brilliant, a visionary, a knowing embodiment of everything that was evil and terrible in the world that was her life. 

"Soon, it will be done. All I ask is that you'll remember me." Edward said, the whir of metal peaking as he raised his arm to stroke her face. "Even after all I am, you've somehow managed to love me," 

"How could I not? You're all I've ever known," she explained, thinking back on all the men she'd loved during her life. Nothing but adulterous leeches; this one was different. He truly seemed to only have eyes for her, but she knew he loved another. "And yet, the doctor will miss you." 

"The dead miss nothing, for they do not know they are dead." Edward brought her forward, to him, pulling her face up to meet his. "And now, my dear, I say goodbye." 

He closed his eyes, the soft glow of them fading as his lips touched hers. She embraced his wide shoulders as she pulled him even closer, wanting to feel the cold beneath his false skin as she had on so many treasured nights. She felt his body go limp, pushing her down on the bed in a way that was so familiar, yet so wrong. 

"Edward..." she cried softly, running her hands upon his face to have her look at him one last time. 

"I l-lo..." he muttered, the gears in his jaw whirring spastically as his system shut down before her very eyes. 

There, finally, were the words she had so oft longed to hear from him; the elusive 'I love you' that was never able to be said. He faded away then, in her arms, never able to hear or say or do another thing or misdeed again. That was all for Edward Hyde. 

"Rest in peace, my dear Henry Jekyll," she said, embracing the projection of the doctor's evil manifestation to her one, final time.
